headline: Brookfield argues legendary music catalogs face minimal AI disruption risk, enhancing their long-term resilience as an asset class
reasoning: Sachin Shah highlights that while AI poses a significant risk to new music creation and emerging artists, legendary catalogs with decades of proven staying power are structurally insulated from this threat. The scarcity value of iconic artists — there is only one James Brown, one Bob Marley, one Whitney Houston — means no AI-generated proxy can substitute for or compete with these assets. This resilience in the face of technological disruption makes legendary music catalogs even more valuable on a long-term view.
quote: Today, in a lot of new music, the talk is about AI, and the good thing with Larry's business, I'm sure he can expand on this, is that when you focus on legendary music, when you focus on legendary artists and songs and artists that have had decades of staying power, there's no AI risk behind that. I think it's even more important that we found Primary Wave and partnered with Larry and the team because of what they do, because its resilience in the midst of a lot of change is what will make this business even more valuable long-term.

headline: Primary Wave expands into name, image, likeness and live touring rights as part of its differentiated royalty monetisation strategy
reasoning: Larry Mustal outlines how Primary Wave has broadened its income streams beyond traditional music publishing royalties and master recordings to include name, image, and likeness rights as well as, in the case of Foreigner's Mick Jones, live touring rights. The Foreigner deal is described as novel because most artists do not relinquish control of their live business. The firm is also pursuing content opportunities such as the Rocky Horror Picture Show deal with the Sphere in Las Vegas, where comparable content like The Wizard of Oz generated nearly $400 million in gross ticket sales. These strategies are designed to convert a $1 royalty dollar into $5 through active alpha creation.
quote: We bought everything from, and I say bought, it's really partnered, because that's already though, it's partnered with the Notorious BIG. We just closed a deal to partner with Pete Townsend in The Who, Britney Spears, The Cars, In Access, John Mellencamp... We just did a deal with Lou Adler. We closed and funded an acquisition of Mick Jones and Foreigners catalog. This is special because not only did we buy music publishing rights and masters and master royalties, but in addition to that, we bought name, image, likeness rights, and for the first time, we actually bought the touring rights, the live rights... Mick wanted to partner with us on the live business, and he owns the trademark to Foreigner. So it's a unique opportunity.

headline: Primary Wave and Brookfield announce acquisition of music publisher Cobalt as the firm accelerates deployment of its $2 billion-plus fund
reasoning: Larry Mustal notes that Primary Wave has been deploying capital faster than anticipated and has just announced the acquisition of Cobalt, described as a 'very sizable music company,' expected to close within 30 days. He credits the Brookfield partnership as essential to executing a transaction of this scale, both for the capital backing and for the credibility it provides to sellers. The firm has also recently partnered with artists including the Notorious B.I.G., Pete Townshend and The Who, Britney Spears, The Cars, John Mellencamp, Axl Rose, Lou Adler, and Mick Jones and Foreigner.
quote: We just announced an acquisition that will be closing sometime in the next 30 days of a very sizable music company called Cobalt. It would have been impossible had we not had the relationship with Brookfield to get through all of what we needed to get through on the transaction and have the capital behind us to say, hey, we're closing. That's really powerful when you're going in and having conversations with potential sellers.

headline: Brookfield's insurance arm committed $1.5-1.6 billion to music royalties, seeing catalog values rise despite the 10-year Treasury moving from 1% to 4.5%
reasoning: Sachin Shah notes that Brookfield invested in Primary Wave when the 10-year US Treasury was at 1% and has since watched rates rise to 4.5% — a period in which music catalog values and cash flows have continued to grow. This rate-insensitivity contrasts sharply with traditional credit, which suffered significant mark-to-market losses over the same period. The long-duration, non-correlated nature of the asset class makes it particularly well-suited for insurance capital, which needs to match long-dated liabilities such as life insurance and annuities.
quote: We invested with Larry, as he said, four and a half years ago when the 10-year treasury in the US, I'm going to get a little nerdy here, was at 1%. Today it's four and a half. So we saw all this rate increase, and yet the value of our catalogs has gone up. The cash flows have gone up. The artists that Larry can bring in continue to come in because of the value the team can create. So where you've seen a lot of destruction maybe is too strong of a word, but where you've seen a lot of issues in the credit space, you've seen none of that in music.

headline: Brookfield sees music royalties as ideal for insurance portfolios given duration match, inflation linkage, and predictable long-term cash flows
reasoning: Sachin Shah explains that insurance companies face the fundamental challenge of predicting cash flows 15 or more years into the future to match long-dated liabilities from life insurance and annuities. Music royalties address this directly: they provide predictable, long-duration income streams with built-in growth from platform rate increases and active brand management. The lack of correlation to interest rates and credit markets gives insurance allocators additional comfort. Brookfield has committed both its own insurance capital and brought insurance clients into the Primary Wave investment.
quote: Most insurance companies have very long dated liabilities, whether you're offering life insurance or annuities. The hardest part of that is having some predictability of cash flow 15 plus years out. This business offers that duration. You have a good sense of what your cash flows will be for the long-term, and you also have a sense that they'll grow so that you're capturing both inflation and real growth, the alpha that Larry talked about. For us, it was a no-brainer to bring our insurance capital into the business supporting growth, and we brought our insurance clients into this business as well.

headline: Primary Wave CEO argues music royalties are superior to traditional credit due to inflation-positive cash flows, long duration, and uncorrelated returns
reasoning: Larry Mustal contends that music royalties outperform standard credit on multiple dimensions. The asset class is inflation-positive because royalty income rises when streaming platforms like Spotify or Apple raise subscription rates. Duration is exceptional — copyright protection extends 70 years past the death of the last writer, generating 35-40 years of visible cash flows. Returns are uncorrelated to markets because music consumption actually increases during periods of global strife. Alpha can be created through active brand management, marketing, and content creation, something most passive royalty collectors do not pursue.
quote: Music royalties are better than credit. They're better than standard credit because the reality is that these assets talking about inflation, they're inflation positive because every time Apple or Spotify or a DSP raises their rates, we're the beneficiary of them raising rates because we get a piece of that. If you look at the characteristics of the asset class, you can't match the duration of music royalties in terms of comparing it to credit because in many cases, songs don't go into public domain for 70 years after the death of the last writer on a song. This is 35, 40 years of ongoing cash flow stories. And also, where do you find credit that's uncorrelated to the market? So our best times are when there's strife in the world and people come to music for comfort, so it's uncorrelated to the markets.

headline: Brookfield views digitalization, decarbonization and deglobalization as accelerating secular mega trends creating unprecedented investment opportunities
reasoning: Brookfield identifies three secular mega trends — digitalization, decarbonization and deglobalization — as accelerating and creating opportunities unlike any seen before. These trends are capital intensive and require multiple capabilities to execute successfully. The nature of investing is changing such that success increasingly depends on combining global relationships, market trend identification, operating expertise and flexible capital. Brookfield has deliberately built these capabilities over time and sees its scale as a key differentiator. As an example, they announced a $100 billion partnership to build one of the most advanced AI factories in Kentucky with the US government.
quote: These trends are accelerating and creating opportunities unlike any seen before. Opportunities that require multiple capabilities to execute successfully. As a result, the nature of investing is changing. Success increasingly depends on the ability to combine global relationships, identification of market trends, operating expertise and flexible capital to deliver integrated solutions at scale. A combination that has become an important characteristic of our business.

headline: Brookfield sees constructive global macro environment with low risk of meaningful rate increases despite near-term inflation from energy prices
reasoning: Despite Middle East conflict and resulting energy supply constraints, the global economy held up well, supported by strong labor markets, consumer spending and AI infrastructure investment. Higher energy prices have added to near-term inflation and led markets to reassess the path of interest rates. However, Brookfield believes central banks will remain cautious rather than aggressive, and the risk of meaningful rate increases appears low. They view temporary market disruptions as distracting from firmly intact longer-term economic fundamentals.
quote: Despite the conflict in the Middle East and the resulting energy supply constraints, the global economy held up well. Strong labor markets, consumer spending and significant investment related to the development of AI infrastructure continue to support economic growth. Higher energy prices have added to near term inflation and led markets to reassess the path of interest rates. While central banks are likely to remain cautious in the near term, the risk of any meaningful increases in interest rates appears to be low. As is often the case, temporary market disruptions have received much of the attention, while the longer term economic fundamentals remain firmly in place.

headline: Brookfield sees accelerating global energy demand and supply constraints creating a structural widening gap that benefits its full-service power solutions platform
reasoning: Global demand for energy is growing rapidly while constraints across grid infrastructure and supply chains are limiting new supply. This is creating a widening gap between power needed and power available. For the largest users of power, securing reliable generation has become a strategic priority requiring balancing cost, scale, speed to market and security of supply. Brookfield has positioned itself as the world's largest full-service provider of power solutions to countries and large corporations, developing approximately 10 gigawatts of new solar and wind generation each year and expanding into batteries, fuel cells and nuclear.
quote: Global demand for energy is growing rapidly, while constraints across grid infrastructure and supply chains are limiting the pace at which new supply can be brought online. The result is a widening gap between the power the world needs and the power available. For the largest users of power, securing reliable generation has become a strategic priority, one that requires balancing cost, scale, speed to market, reliability, and security of supply. We are seeing this play out across our energy and infrastructure businesses, where we have become the world's largest full-service provider of power solutions to countries and to the largest and fastest-growing companies.

headline: Brookfield sees Westinghouse as uniquely positioned to lead the next wave of nuclear deployment with unassailable moat as sovereigns and large power buyers commit to nuclear at scale
reasoning: Westinghouse is Brookfield's leading global nuclear services business whose technology is used by over half of the world's operating nuclear reactors and which services roughly half of the global reactor fleet. Energy security is moving to the center of strategic decision-making as sovereigns and large power buyers plan long-term energy needs, driving large, long-duration commitments to baseload nuclear generation. The US Department of Energy recently announced a $17.5 billion commitment to finance long lead time equipment for 10 new large-scale reactors, which will materially lower execution risks and shorten development timelines. Westinghouse stands to benefit from growth in recurring services as existing reactors are life-extended and from building the next generation of reactors.
quote: Westinghouse is our leading global nuclear services business. Its technology is used by over half of the world's operating nuclear reactors. Yes, over half of all in the world. The company also services roughly half of the global reactor fleet, with the majority of its cash flows generated from occurring fuel supply and maintenance services... Nuclear is increasingly central to these plans, providing reliable, carbon-free, baseload power that few other technologies can match. Through Westinghouse, we are leading the next wave of nuclear deployment... As the lives of existing reactors are extended and the largest nuclear build-out in decades gains momentum, Westinghouse stands to benefit significantly, growth from the growth of its recurring services business and from building the next generation of nuclear reactors. Few businesses in the world today have such significant structural tier ones for growth and a moat which is unassailable.

headline: Brookfield completes capital structure simplification combining insurance and investment capabilities under a single BN entity, seen as creating a stronger platform for index inclusion and growth
reasoning: Shareholders approved the simplification of Brookfield's capital structure, combining insurance and investment capabilities into a single entity trading under BN on NYSE and TSX. The simplified structure is expected to strengthen eligibility for inclusion in major US and global equity indices, which should improve trading liquidity, broaden the shareholder base and improve accessibility. The combination is designed to position Brookfield for its next phase of growth without changing the overall investment strategy.
quote: The combination gives us a stronger structure through which to pursue our long term goals. As our wealth solutions business continues to grow, it is becoming an increasingly important source of long duration capital, a complement to our leading asset management business and together position us well to invest at scale in the mega trends shaping the global economy. The new simplified structure will also strengthen our ability for inclusion in major US and global equity indices and added benefit that did not exist before. And as index investing continues to grow, this should improve accessibility, increase trading liquidity and broaden our shareholder base.

headline: Brookfield completes full acquisition of Oaktree, creating one of the world's most comprehensive credit platforms with expanded US presence
reasoning: Brookfield completed the acquisition of the remaining interest in Oaktree, fully integrating it after a seven-year partnership. The combined entity now has one of the world's most comprehensive credit platforms spanning real asset, asset-backed and opportunistic credit. The transaction significantly expands Brookfield's US presence, with more than 60% of investment and asset management employees now based in the US. Brookfield believes Oaktree's expertise in distressed and opportunistic credit, combined with Brookfield's scale and global relationships, positions the platform well to exploit upcoming dislocation opportunities in credit markets.
quote: When we first partnered in 2019, we brought together Oaktree's disciplined investment approach and world-class expertise in distress and opportunistic credit with our scale capital, global relationships and operating capabilities. The partnership worked very well. Combined, we now have one of the world's most comprehensive credit platforms spanning real asset, asset-backed and opportunistic credit. Bringing the organizations fully together strengthens our ability to serve clients with a broader range of investment solutions while preserving the distinct qualities that have made Oaktree successful.

headline: Views the opening of the $14 trillion US defined contribution market to private assets as a multi-decade structural shift and a major new source of long-term capital
reasoning: Changes to US federal policy are clearing a path for private markets to enter defined contribution retirement plans. The US DC market is approximately $14 trillion of retirement savings, meaning even modest allocations to private assets have the potential to create one of the largest new sources of long-term capital for the alternatives industry. Individual savers have historically lacked access to private assets that large pension plans, endowments and sovereign wealth funds have long used to compound capital. Businesses today also stay private far longer than before, meaning investors in only public securities are participating in a shrinking share of global value creation. Brookfield has positioned itself for this opportunity through a collaboration with AllianceBernstein to provide access to its strategies for custom defined contribution plans.
quote: Changes to US federal policy are now clearing a path for private markets. This is an important step. The US defined contribution market is approximately $14 trillion of retirement savings, meaning even modest allocations to private assets have the potential to create one of the largest new sources of long-term capital for our industry. We are ready for this evolution. Our platform is built around real assets and essential service businesses that offer the income, capital stability, and inflation protection that long-term retirement and wealth portfolios require... This is not a short-term opportunity. It is a multi-decade shift in how retirement capital will be invested.

headline: Brookfield expands Bloom Energy partnership five-fold to up to $25 billion to accelerate deployment of behind-the-meter fuel cell power solutions for data centers
reasoning: Brookfield increased the size of its framework with Bloom Energy five-fold to invest up to $25 billion to accelerate deployment of behind-the-meter fuel cell projects for data centers. This technology provides one of the fastest-to-market sources of continuous 24/7 power available and is seen as an important part of the future power mix. The partnership is part of Brookfield's broader strategy to be a full-service power provider, capitalising on the structural gap between growing energy demand and constrained supply.
quote: Nowhere is this more evident than in the expansion of our partnership with Bloom Energy, where we increase the size of our framework five-fold to invest up to $25 billion to accelerate the deployment of behind-the-meter fuel cell projects for data centers. This technology provides one of the fastest-to-market sources of continuous, 24-7 power solutions available today and will be an important part of the future power mix for years to come.

headline: Brookfield sees private credit stress concentrated in sponsor-backed software lending as a healthy adjustment, not a systemic problem, while its own credit book remains well-positioned
reasoning: Much attention has been paid to risks in private credit, particularly direct lending to sponsor-led private equity backed borrowers with exposure to software businesses. Brookfield's credit franchise is concentrated in real asset finance, asset-backed lending and opportunistic credit, with limited exposure to the sectors under pressure. The firm kept leverage modest and underwriting selective, which has protected the portfolio. Brookfield views the current environment as a healthy adjustment following a period of overly loose underwriting, not a systemic problem, and sees dislocation as creating attractive opportunities for Oaktree's distressed and opportunistic credit capabilities.
quote: Much has been written lately about the risks in private credit. Concerned center on direct lending to sponsor-led private equity backed borrowers and exposure to software businesses. Our credit franchise is concentrated in areas where we have deep expertise. Real asset finance, asset-backed lending and opportunistic credit. We have grown the business thoughtfully and maintained our investment discipline, leaving us with limited exposure to the sectors and investor channels currently under the greatest pressure. Lending against the same types of assets and businesses that we own and operate gives us a better understanding of asset values, cash flows and downside risk... We do not view today's environment as a systemic problem and the areas attracting the most attention represent only a very small part of the broader credit market. What we are seeing is merely a healthy adjustment following a period in which abundant capital led underwriting standards to become too loose in parts of the market.

headline: Brookfield finding cross-portfolio AI use cases in industrial and renewables businesses, including machine vision, supply chain optimisation, and wind asset maintenance
reasoning: David Bonacie highlights that Brookfield's private equity industrial portfolio companies share common AI use cases around machine vision and quality control, supply chain and inventory optimisation, and asset maintenance. In the renewables portfolio, AI use cases identified in one wind business have proven highly fungible and are being replicated quickly across other portfolio companies. He notes that back-office functions such as finance, procurement, customer support, and asset management are common across all Brookfield platforms — real estate, renewables, and private equity — enabling a scalable, cross-platform approach to AI value creation.
quote: If you think in our private equity business, we own many industrial companies. There's a lot of common use cases across machine vision and quality, supply chain and inventory optimization, and asset maintenance. That's been great. Maybe another example, if I take our renewables business, we have many portfolio companies that are wind renewable businesses. We've found use cases in one business that we can actually have our other portfolio companies replicate very quickly. They're very fungible. That's how we're thinking about how do we bring the Brookfield ecosystem to bear.

headline: Brookfield sees enormous long-term TAM in AI enterprise deployment, analogising to decades-long ERP services market
reasoning: David Bonacie draws a parallel to ERP technology, which has been around for 40 years yet most enterprises still require outside help to deploy it, suggesting AI deployment services represent a structural, multi-decade opportunity rather than a short-term gap. He notes that in technology markets, for every dollar of technology spend, deployment and services revenue typically attaches at multiples and is often recurring or semi-recurring. The combination of frontier AI advancing rapidly and enterprises consistently needing help to extract maximum value means demand for deployment capability should grow alongside the technology itself. This underpins both the strategic rationale and the expected economic returns of the DeployCo investment.
quote: I would look more at historically what's happened with certain large-scale technologies. So if you think about ERPs, which have been around for 40 years, enormous companies have been built off of nothing other than deploying ERP technology and enterprise. And it's lasted many decades. And even today, most companies don't know how to deploy an ERP in their organization. Even today, technology has been around for 40 years. Most of us still have to call in someone to come in and deploy that technology in our organization for us. And so I think there is a huge runway and a huge opportunity for actually implementing AI in enterprise, which is not a short-term gap. It's a long-term gap that's going to exist forever.

headline: AI infrastructure and enterprise deployment are two sides of the same flywheel — infrastructure enables adoption while adoption drives more infrastructure demand
reasoning: Anuj Ranjan frames AI infrastructure build-out and enterprise deployment as mutually reinforcing rather than competing priorities. Infrastructure is required to enable adoption, but as enterprise adoption scales it creates further demand for infrastructure, creating a self-reinforcing cycle. This view contextualises Brookfield's broader infrastructure and deployment investments as complementary exposures to the same secular AI growth theme.
quote: Infrastructure and deployment are, I think, two sides of the same AI flywheel. We need infrastructure to enable adoption, but as that adoption scales, it creates more demand for infrastructure. And so this is really a flywheel that sits tandem and hand-in-hand with each other. The two sides, the same coin.

headline: Brookfield PE invests in OpenAI's DeployCo, betting AI value creation shifts from model quality to enterprise deployment capability
reasoning: Anuj Ranjan argues that the AI race has shifted from model invention to execution, with the bottleneck no longer being what the technology can do but whether companies can embed it into daily workflows and generate measurable business outcomes. Brookfield's thesis is that AI value will accrue to the best implementers, not the biggest spenders, with the combination of OpenAI's frontier model capability and Brookfield's deep operating expertise forming a powerful differentiator. The TAM is seen as enormous, drawing an analogy to ERP deployment where service and deployment revenues typically run at multiples of technology spend and are often recurring. Brookfield sees a one-to-three year payback horizon as the preferred discipline for AI projects, with only high-conviction, high-value cases justifying longer durations.
quote: I think AI value will accrue now to the best implementers, not just the biggest spenders in technology. What gets a lot of headlines is it's a CapEx arms race. That's true. But those who implement the technology best across their portfolio, I think, is where you'll see the most benefits, the productivity gains, and the most value creation. We genuinely think the companies that will create the most value from AI will not be the ones that spend the most money on it. It'll be the ones that use it best with the right data, the right governance, the right operating discipline, and the right change management.

headline: E-commerce demand driving logistics leasing across APAC, with Coupang anchoring CLC as Korea's dominant platform
reasoning: Coupang, described as the Amazon equivalent in Korea, was secured as the anchor tenant for approximately 40% of CLC's space, with the majority of the facility utilised for e-commerce. The team credits close tenant engagement — including weekly or biweekly conversations — with enabling them to adapt the asset (e.g. converting cold storage to dry warehousing, installing new power for automation) to meet evolving e-commerce requirements and achieve 100% occupancy.
quote: What was unique about and interesting about this deal was that we were able to secure an anchor tenant with coupon, which is the Amazon equivalent in Korea. And so the majority of the space is utilized for e-commerce. Something we're increasingly familiar with, I would say around the world.

headline: Brookfield actively looking at office deals in Korea as fundamentals remain attractive
reasoning: Despite broader global office market headwinds, Brookfield's Korea team is currently evaluating several office transactions, suggesting they see value in the Korean office market. The team highlights familiarity with the market and on-the-ground capability as enabling factors.
quote: We like other sectors in the Korean market. We're looking at a few office deals.

headline: Brookfield prioritising the living sector in Korea and across APAC as a key expansion theme
reasoning: Brookfield is actively working to establish a presence in the residential/living sector in Korea and more broadly across APAC. This is described as a strategic focus area the team is trying to 'crack', indicating it is an emerging priority rather than an established business line in the region.
quote: And then we've been really trying to crack the living sector in Korea. And even just outside of Korea, we're really looking to build on the living sector across all of APAC as well. So I would say that's where we're focusing our time in Korea, but more broadly in Asia, it's a lot of the same themes we're seeing, as we're seeing in Korea.

headline: Brookfield bullish on Korean hotel sector as tourism surges but international brand supply remains scarce
reasoning: Korea is experiencing strong tourism growth but lacks sufficient hotel capacity, particularly from international brands. This supply-demand imbalance is seen as a compelling backdrop for rent and rate growth. Brookfield identifies hotels as an area with very good fundamentals in the current Korean market environment.
quote: We think the fundamentals for hotels are incredibly good right now. There's not a lot of international brands. There's not enough hotel space for the amount of tourism that Korea is seeing. So it's a good backdrop for rent growth there.

headline: Brookfield sees strong logistics fundamentals in Korea as a key APAC real estate growth market
reasoning: Brookfield opened a Korean office over a decade ago and made its first Seoul acquisition in 2016, viewing Korea as a key market for real estate growth. The team highlights strong GDP growth, attractive fundamentals in logistics and office, and the advantage of having an on-the-ground operating and investment team without reliance on local partners. Korea is described as a developed APAC economy with compelling sector-level dynamics.
quote: Korea's a established economy in APAC. It's one of the developed markets. We see good GDP growth in the country. There's a lot of factors that make it an attractive place to invest. The fundamentals for some of the sectors that we like, including logistics, including office, makes sense for us. We've got familiarity. We've got a team on the ground, both on the operating side, but also on the investment side. And so we're able to actually execute on business plans ourselves and not really rely on local operating partners.

headline: Brookfield pursuing distressed Korean logistics assets and rescue financing as oversupply creates acquisition opportunities
reasoning: A wave of new logistics supply in Korea over recent years has led to leasing difficulties and financing stress for developers who used excessive leverage. Brookfield sees this as an opportunity to buy distressed loans with a view to acquiring equity control, or to provide rescue financing to developers. This pipeline of stressed assets is described as a key current focus for the Korea team.
quote: In the Korean market, we touched a little bit on the extra supply that came on over the last few years in the logistics space. And what has happened as a result is that there's been some liquidity issues in some of the other assets that haven't been able to lease up that don't have the sort of same experience or expertise that we have. I would also say that a lot of the Korean developers, they used a lot more leverage than we would typically see in other markets. So that's led to a bunch of stress in the market on the financing side. So what we've actually been doing, we've been spending a lot of time is looking at ways to either buy loans with the view to getting control of the equity or providing rescue loans to various developers. And that's been a great area for building out our pipeline.

headline: Brookfield constructive on APAC real estate broadly, citing strong GDP growth relative to other regions
reasoning: The team frames its Korean and broader APAC real estate investment activity in the context of strong regional GDP growth, which they view as a tailwind for real estate demand across logistics, office, hotels and living. APAC is presented as relatively more attractive than other global regions on a GDP growth basis.
quote: Well, and buoyed by a lot of that strong GDP growth in the region relative maybe to others, there's a lot of opportunity there.

headline: Network International building crypto-as-a-service for financial institutions and enabling stablecoin and cryptocurrency acceptance at point-of-sale, with UAE leading regional regulatory framework.
reasoning: Marat separated the crypto opportunity into two segments: financial institutions that want to offer crypto custody, exchange and KYC-integrated services to their customers, and merchants that want to accept crypto and stablecoin payments without missing sales. Network is providing turnkey crypto infrastructure to banks and is working with UAE regulators to enable crypto acceptance at its merchant terminals. The speaker highlighted that with dominant market share across multiple countries, Network could become a key distribution partner for stablecoin providers and central bank digital currencies seeking to grow point-of-sale usage.
quote: For financial institutions, they would like to offer crypto services to their customers. And for those financial institutions, we are already integrated to their core platform as a payments company, as a payments infrastructure provider, which means we are already doing millions of transactions per day for a bank... What's coming up with crypto is that some of those customers, they would like to do custody of that crypto in their main financial institution. They would like to build exchange in that finance institution as well... we are providing crypto as a service. It's a turnkey solution. If a bank approaches us and says, I would like to offer crypto to my customers, we have our own ecosystem of partners that we have integrated already.

headline: Brookfield views payments infrastructure as an 'infinite pipeline' for digital money movement, with a data monetisation layer that significantly expands the investment thesis beyond pure transaction processing.
reasoning: Anuj Ranjan explained to Brookfield's investment committee that payments infrastructure resembles a pipeline for moving money, but unlike physical infrastructure it has unlimited capacity. The initial thesis centred on the scalability of digital rails, but the more transformative realisation has been the data layer sitting on top of payments — enabling merchants, banks, governments and businesses to extract intelligence from transaction flows. This evolution from payments-as-process to payments-as-data-platform is seen as analogous to Google's transformation from a search engine into a data moat business.
quote: I remember when we made our first investment in Magnati that eventually led to network and led to the combination of the two. We had to explain it to our board, to our investment committee, to the field's largest infrastructure owner in the world. So I still remember that slide. We drew a pipeline and we showed all the different components of the payments ecosystem. On a pipeline, it said it's like a pipe that moves any commodity except what it's moving is money. It's moving money in the digital pipeline. But the big benefit of it and the thing we were most excited about is unlike a physical pipeline, which has a fixed capacity, here the capacity was unlimited, was infinite. You could move as much money as possible through these pipelines.

headline: Payments ecosystem evolving toward borderless, real-time, data-rich infrastructure with significant government-backed digitisation tailwinds across Middle East and Africa.
reasoning: Marat Charu Souser described a two-part evolution: payments themselves are becoming faster, more convenient and increasingly borderless (cross-border transfers now taking 2–5 seconds), and payments companies are building additional FinTech services on top of their infrastructure. Governments across the region are actively partnering with payments providers to digitise their economies, and mobile wallets have dramatically expanded financial inclusion across Africa. The combination of government support, scale advantages, and data monetisation potential represents a structural growth opportunity for incumbents with broad licensing and network reach.
quote: What we see in the region is more and more there is effort from governments, very thoughtful efforts from governments, on digitizing the economy. And payments is a key pillar of it. So as payment companies, we are part of the initiative, we are working very actively with governments in terms of how to digitize the economies. And it has very beneficial impacts to businesses and consumers. As you see in Africa, for example, in the past, during the global penetration of the Beijing population, it was very hard to do payments. And now in the past few years, through mobile wallets, anyone can do payments anywhere, anytime in most of Africa without the need to hold the plastic, to hold the credit card in their pockets.

headline: Generative AI doubling developer productivity at Network International within one month, while AI has underpinned fraud detection in payments for over 15 years.
reasoning: Marat noted that AI in the form of machine learning has been core to payments fraud detection for 15+ years given the impossibility of human review of 1,000+ transactions per second. The newer generative AI layer is now accelerating product development — developer productivity doubled within one month of deployment — and enabling better customer segmentation through synthetic data generation. AI is also being deployed in IVR customer service agents, handling 35% of call centre needs autonomously. The speaker views AI as a structural productivity and capability multiplier for payments infrastructure companies.
quote: With generative AI, there are two things that are significantly improving. Now with generative AI, it can generate its own data. So even with small amounts of data, we can generate very strong works, which means we can segment more and we can serve better. Now there is the other piece of AI where it increases the productivity. We see the impact of it on our developers, testers first. So we started testing it some time ago and then immediately after one month only... we doubled the productivity just while I'm on our developers. So now the amount of products that we can put into the market, speed and convenience, so then increase significant.

headline: Brookfield Private Equity built regional payments champion through combination of Magnati and Network International, operating across 56 countries in Middle East and Africa.
